title: Four Sources of Laughter
paragraphs: ( The term eḷḷal (ridicule), one of the sources of laughter, has been in vogue for a very long time) Commentators bring in the example of a lame person while talking about the situations where ridicule is due.

( Humane considerations prohibit ridiculing others especially the handicapped. The fast spreading social awareness in the modern world rules out ridicule of a handicapped person’s staggering being a source of laughter.)
However, I would like to share with you an incident I have heard of as an example of the source of laughter.

It was an incident that occurred in a city. Even as civilization has seen great advancement with the advent of industrialization and electrification, people were travelling in bullock carts and carriages driven by horses. There was a vegetable vendor who did business on the roadside. People regularly bought vegetables from him. Whenever a cart passed by, the vendor would become enraged and challenge the occupant with swear words. He would shout, “Hey, horse carriage, bullock cart, go slowly. Why on earth do you raise dust while whizzing past the road? If I get up and come there, you might have to meet with dire consequences. I would whip you severely.”
Though none of the vehicle owners cared to listen to him, the vendor never stopped hurling abuses.

One fine day, the vendor shouted and threatened the driver of a horse carriage as was his wont. “Do you know what I would do? I will break your carriage to pieces. Why do you stare? Do you know what will happen if I come there?” Just as the vendor was at his abusive best, the driver stopped the carriage and dared him to come near.
The vendor was dumbstruck. The reason being his inability to do so, as he was handicapped, without legs.
This evoked laughter from all quarters.
(Ridicule suits only such particular situations. It does not suit the disabled in general, neither should it do so.)
(Since Pāṇṭiyaṉ Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ was young, he was mocked at by the other kings. An undaunted Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ rose up in arms against them. My poem below celebrates the exploits of this youth: )
The jingling anklet on the leg of this tender youth Was replaced by a string of bells marking heroism.
The plaited lock was cut off. He was a boy-king holding a dazzling sword.
He took off the bangles from his tender hands And sported the bow on his shoulder. He was still an adolescent wearing amulet.
Therefore, holding him too young, The two crowned monarchs, Cēra and Cōḻa. Together with the five mighty vēḷir chieftains challenged him for a war.

The famous army of the five chieftains paired with The kings holding the banners sporting arrow and tiger, The young Pāṇṭiyaṉ was never perturbed At the event of crossing swords with the alliance of the seven.
Looking at the message from the enemy, “Better be chastised, otherwise you may have to part with very life,” He laughed aloud and roared: “It is not in our tradition to hide from war.
Do you think that the Pāṇṭiya kingdom is a place of recluses? No, no, it is not so. Our presiding deity Mother Pāṇṭi has not begotten cowards.
Oh! Countrymen! Virtuous souls! Trust me. This young Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ would add to the fame of our motherland Thus did the young king instil valour into his subjects.
The foes looked down upon the youth and mocked him. He in turn laughed at their arrogance and it was he who had the last laugh.
A person preferred a written complaint to the police station about the theft of a metal pot (tavalai)
The police official peered through and burst out laughing, “But then your head is very much intact.”
Owing to poor knowledge, he missed the letter ‘va’ and has instead written talai in his complaint.
Just as the official explained, he also joined in the laughter, got back his petition and made the correction.
The official laughed again and enquired, “Pray, from which well did the frog disappear?”
Again, instead of tavalai he had mistakenly written tavaḷai meaning frog.
So ignorant was he that after having made the pot a head, he now has made it a frog.
These four are then situations and objects that have the potential to provoke laughter. Here is the Tolkāppiyam verse:
> The four sources of laughter are > Ridicule, childishness, stupidity and credulity.
(Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 4)
